visible.summary:
Portugal remains one of the world's safest destinations for transgender visitors. The 2018 self-determination law allows legal gender and name change without medical requirements (minors 16-17 with parental consent), bathroom access matching one's gender is legally protected, conversion therapy is banned (2024), intersex infant surgery is banned, and hate-crime law covers gender identity — within an EU rule-of-law environment with very low violent crime. Same-sex marriage since 2010.

Two caveats pull it just below its Iberian neighbour Spain. First, in March 2026 the Portuguese parliament approved in first reading three bills (backed by the governing PSD/CDS and the far-right Chega) that would repeal the 2018 self-ID law, reintroduce a mandatory medical opinion, and ban hormones for minors. As of the most recent reporting this is not yet final law — it is in committee, and a government technical opinion warned it may be unconstitutional — so the self-ID framework is still in force. Second, hate-crime reports rose about 38% in both 2023 and 2024, with acknowledged under-reporting.

For a visitor these translate to a real political-hostility signal and elevated but still low-level harassment risk, not criminal exposure. The practical day-to-day environment is calm and welcoming, particularly in Lisbon and Porto.
visible.tangentialFactors: Same-sex marriage since 2010 — relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners.
visible.localsOnly: The 2018 self-ID law, the 2026 repeal attempt (in committee), and the minors' hormone ban proposal are resident-facing; the intersex infant surgery ban is a resident protection.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Petty theft in tourist areas and a general terrorism guidance footnote affect all travellers.

sources.claim: ILGA-Europe Rainbow Map 2026: Portugal drops one place to 12th at 67%; no affirmative legislation since the 2024 conversion-practices ban, while a new draft bill threatens legal gender recognition based on self-determination and the ban on forced medical interventions on intersex children. No score 67% below Malta/Iceland/Belgium but above most of Europe.
Público (March 2026, in Portuguese): the Portuguese Parliament (AR) approved PSD, Chega and CDS bills reversing the gender-identity law - first vote to roll back self-ID legal gender recognition.

Observador (Mar 2026): parliament debates rolling back the gender-identity regime; psychologists' order and trans groups call it 'retrocesso'; socialists invoked the 2006 murder of Gisberta (trans woman killed by youths in Porto) against the rollback, drawing protests from Chega's Hugo Soares. Documents the political fight around the three roll-back bills.

Joint statement: IGLYO, ILGA-Europe, OII Europe, TGEU, EL*C and Bi+ Equal warn three bills debated 19 March, voted 20 March 2026 would seriously attack trans/intersex rights, bodily autonomy and legal gender recognition; if adopted Portugal would lose at least 4 Rainbow Map places, dropping below Sweden, Netherlands, Ireland and France - regression from a European reference point.

Forbidden Colours (20 Mar 2026): Parliament passed the roll-back proposals 124 to 79 (backed by Chega, governing PSD and CDS-PP), sending them to the Committee on Rights, Freedoms and Guarantees; the proposals directly target Portugal's 2018 self-identification law. Called a dangerous turning point for fundamental rights.

KET Brussels (26 Mar 2026): in first reading Parliament backed reintroducing a mandatory medical opinion for any legal gender and name change, undoing the 2018 reform that allowed self-declaration from age 16; human rights groups say it is dismantling the self-determination law.

TVI/IOL: committee-stage analysis (CIG) of the bills warns they worsen suffering and negative outcomes for trans people and defends schools' existing discrimination-prevention duties; Bloco de Esquerda bill assessed as compatible with school human-rights obligations. Legislative-process detail on the roll-back package.

The Portugal Brief (16 Aug 2026): Justice Ministry data show legal sex/name changes climbing back toward the two-years-prior high-water mark, most in Lisbon (per Expresso) - even as Parliament advances bills to reimpose the medical requirement the 2018 self-determination law scrapped. Uptick before the expected tightening.

European Parliament written question E-001183/2026 (2026), 'Health and safety of transgender people in Portugal' — an MEP questions the Commission on the repeal process for the 2018 gender self-determination law and its health-and-safety impact on trans people.

OSCE hate-crime legislation portal, Portugal: Penal Code makes sexual orientation and gender identity/explicit grounds for aggravated offences - Art. 132/144/145 aggravation when crime determined by hatred on those grounds (aggravated assault up to 4 years), plus 1-8 year penalties for organising discrimination on those grounds or genocide-denial-style apology. Legal framework reference.

Equaldex data for Portugal: homosexuality legal, marriage legal, gender change with no restrictions, gender-affirming care legal, full ban on intersex infant surgery, hate-crime protections cover SOGI, discrimination illegal, conversion therapy banned, bathroom access protected. High public support for same-sex parenting (ranked #1 of 30 EU regions).

Provedoria da Justica (Ombudsman): requests constitutional review of Penal Code Article 176-C, which establishes the crime of acts contrary to sexual orientation, gender identity or gender expression - the institutional watchdog questioning the hate-speech provision itself.

visible.summary:
Belgium is a top-tier destination for transgender visitors. Legal gender and name change by self-declaration has been available since 2018, anti-discrimination law covers gender identity and expression across employment, housing and services, hate crime and hate speech are both criminalised for gender identity, and transphobia is a separately tracked hate-crime motive. Belgium also passed Europe's first femicide law (2023), with protections for gender minorities.

The framework is politically stable with no rollback movement — a contrast with several neighbours (the UK's in-force facilities code, Portugal's first-reading repeal attempt, Germany's repeal review). The main caveat is a documented rise in anti-LGBTQ violence and intimidation: the equality body Unia reported in 2025 that gay men and transgender people are increasingly targeted, and an RTBF investigation documented dating-app ambush attacks on queer men in urban nightlife.

For a visitor this is a comfortable environment with the usual urban-nightlife caution: zero legal exposure, functioning institutions, and a welcoming day-to-day climate, particularly in Brussels.
visible.tangentialFactors: Dating-app ambush attacks on queer men documented in urban nightlife — a caution for trans visitors using apps.
visible.localsOnly: The self-declaration LGR process (since 2018, with the constitutional reform that removed the former forced-divorce requirement) is a resident-facing administrative procedure.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: No trans-specific travel advisory; ordinary urban crime in Brussels affects all tourists.

sources.claim: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): Belgium has robust protections - discrimination, hate crimes and hate speech on grounds of SOGISC banned; same-sex marriage and adoption; legal name and gender-marker change based on self-determination. Europe's first femicide law (2023) covers all gender-based homicide; a 2023 law bans conversion practices. Medically unnecessary surgeries on intersex infants remain legal, though a Brussels court held a hospital accountable for nonconsensual interventions.

ILGA-Europe Rainbow Map country page for Belgium: overall index score plus per-category compliance (legal gender recognition, hate crime, equality & non-discrimination, family, civil society, asylum, intersex) — the formal-law snapshot of Belgium's framework.

VRT NWS (May 2025): despite Belgium's progressive reputation, equality bodies Unia and the Institute for the Equality of Women and Men report rising violence and intimidation targeting LGBTQI people, with gay men and trans people especially affected. Of 136 sexual-orientation discrimination cases handled by Unia in a year, 35% involved physical assault and 35% serious intimidation. A recurring pattern is 'dating app traps' - gay men lured via apps, ambushed, beaten and robbed; a high-profile case against three men accused of targeting at least eight victims went to Brussels Criminal Court in May 2025.

KET Magazine (Feb 2025) summarising an RTBF investigation into rising homophobic attacks in Belgium orchestrated through dating apps: perpetrators use fake profiles to arrange meetings, then ambush victims in isolated locations where they are robbed, humiliated or assaulted. Police have recorded an alarming number of incidents, many unreported due to fear or shame.

OSCE/ODIHR page on Belgium's national hate-crime frameworks: hate crimes are not defined in Belgian legislation and no code exists to record them as such; violations of non-discrimination law that constitute criminal offences are prosecuted under general provisions instead.

Official Brussels-Capital Region page on changing gender registration on ID cards: free of charge, 3-6 weeks processing, requires a valid identity document, a medical certificate attesting to sex change, and possibly a judicial or administrative decision; application made in person at the commune, digital mode available.

Belgian Federal Justice Department page: since 1 January 2018 (Law of 25 June 2017), trans people can change registered gender and first names without medical conditions, via a declaration to the civil registrar. On 19 June 2019 the Constitutional Court partially annulled the law; pending new provisions, applications continue under the current procedure.

Intrepid Travel country guide: Belgium is 'one of the safest and most welcoming destinations for LGBTQIA+ travellers in the world', with forward-thinking attitudes and thriving queer culture in Brussels, Antwerp and Liège.

Discovering Belgium guide (2024): overview of LGBT+ rights history and current status - sex between men decriminalised as far back as 1795 under the French penal code, though public-indecency laws and police harassment persisted; covers key figures, organisations, current rights, and where to report homophobia.

'Being transgender in Belgium - Ten years later' (2017), by Motmans, Wyverkens, Defreyne et al. for the Institute for the Equality of Women and Men: a large survey study of trans people in Belgium covering gender identity, coming out, openness, obstacles to living according to one's gender identity, being addressed per experienced gender, official name/gender registration change, work, sex work, economic status and well-being.

Press release (May 2017, in Dutch) from Justice Minister Koen Geens on Belgium's new transgender law: self-determination is the starting point - legal gender change via a purely administrative procedure with all medical conditions (including sterilisation/surgery) scrapped; includes a reflection period and public-order safeguards; notes name-change requests rose from 85 (2012) to 187 (2016).

visible.summary:
Switzerland is a very safe destination for transgender visitors. Legal gender recognition has worked by self-declaration since January 2022 — a personal declaration before the civil registrar, with no court or medical requirements (binary male/female only; no non-binary marker). Same-sex marriage has been legal since 2022 (approved by referendum), gender-neutral rape law took effect in 2024, and employers have a legal duty of care toward trans employees. General crime is exceptionally low.

The notable legislative shortcoming — flagged by the ILGA Rainbow Map and by the government's own review — is that the criminal hate-crime and hate-speech provision (Article 261bis) covers sexual orientation but not gender identity. So a person targeted specifically for being trans does not benefit from that aggravation in criminal law, though the protections available through employment and constitutional law are broader. Reported hate crimes against LGBTIQ people have risen about fivefold since 2020 (around six per week, but from a low absolute base of ~309 cases in 2024).

The federal government adopted Switzerland's first National Action Plan against LGBTIQ hate crime in January 2026 (running to 2030), signalling a pro-trans institutional direction. There is no rollback movement.
visible.tangentialFactors: Same-sex marriage legal since 2022 — relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners.
visible.localsOnly: The self-declaration LGR process (binary only, no non-binary marker) and the employer duty of care are resident-facing administrative/employment law.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Switzerland's principal travel risks (mountain/alpine hazards, road safety) affect all travellers.

sources.claim: Swiss Federal Office for Gender Equality rights overview: since 1 July 2020 public incitement to hatred, denigration or discrimination on sexual-orientation grounds is punishable under Art. 261bis Criminal Code; 'Marriage for All' has been in force since 1 July 2022 (same-sex marriage, adoption, IVF). Freshness pass confirms both pages current.

EPFL guidance on the Swiss civil status register: since 1 January 2022 any person registered in a Swiss municipality can change their sex marker and/or first name by personal declaration before a civil registrar — a self-declaration route without surgery or court proceedings.

SWI swissinfo (7 Aug 2022): about 350 people had used the simplified self-declaration gender-change process introduced on 1 January 2022 within its first months — early uptake of the new marker-change route.

SWI swissinfo, citing LGBTIQ Helpline monitoring: roughly six anti-LGBTIQ+ hate crimes are reported per week in Switzerland — 309 cases in the reference year, with reports up fivefold since 2020. The main day-to-day safety signal for visitors.

Federal Office for Gender Equality: on 28 January 2026 the Federal Council adopted Switzerland's first National Action Plan against hate crimes against LGBTIQ persons 2026-2030, with three pillars — support and protection of victims, prevention of hate crime, and monitoring of violence; FOGE coordinates implementation.

SWI swissinfo on the same first national action plan (2026): coverage of the government's new measures to protect LGBTQI+ people from hate crimes — dated press corroboration of the federal plan and of the rising-report context that prompted it.

LegalClarity (3 Jun 2026): marriage equality since 1 July 2022 after 64.1% referendum approval; criminal-law protection against sexual-orientation discrimination since July 2020; streamlined legal gender change since January 2022 — 'from marriage equality to gender recognition, but some gaps remain'.

trans welcome (Switzerland) workplace legal framework: employers must protect employees' personal dignity under Art. 328ff. Code of Obligations, concretised for trans people by the Equality Act (GLG); trans staff may use their preferred name and gender at work without any official document change.
ILGA-Europe Rainbow Map country page for Switzerland: overall index score and per-category compliance breakdown (after the 2021 self-determination and discrimination votes).

OSCE/ODIHR 2024 Hate Crime Report for Switzerland: Switzerland regularly reports hate-crime data; the Criminal Code has no general hate-crime provision - hate crimes are addressed under anti-discrimination provisions (Art. 261bis); ODIHR notes recording does not sufficiently distinguish hate crimes and police do not record bias motivation.

UNHCR Switzerland, non-discrimination page: everyone in Switzerland has the right to equal treatment; discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited; LGBTIQ+ people enjoy equal rights and same-sex couples can marry since 1 July 2022.

visible.summary:
Austria is a workable destination with a notably more conservative climate and a live far-right government hostility signal. The governing Freedom Party (FPÖ) mocks gender-diverse people publicly and has pledged a constitutional "two sexes" definition that would repeal non-binary protections — a threat, not yet enacted.

The most concrete traveler-relevant risk is organised dating-app predation: in 2025 authorities uncovered a neo-Nazi network that lured, beat, humiliated and filmed victims — primarily gay and bisexual men — through fake dating profiles (15 arrested). Caution is warranted on dating apps for queer travelers. There is no bathroom restriction law, no cross-dressing statute, and no documented border-police humiliation of trans travelers.

If detained, there are no specific legal protections for trans detainees — they are housed with the general population on an ad-hoc basis (only three trans people were in detention as of mid-2025). Trans-specific hate incidents actually declined in 2025, though homophobic violence rose.
visible.tangentialFactors: The dating-app predation network targeted gay and bisexual men primarily — a risk for trans visitors using apps, though not trans-specific.
visible.localsOnly: Legal gender recognition runs through the courts (the Constitutional Court affirmed gender identity as protected in December 2025) — a resident-facing process.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: General urban crime is low; the high cost of living is a non-safety travel note.

sources.claim: ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 (covering 2025) chapter on Austria. Documents a neo-Nazi network uncovered in March that used fake dating profiles to lure gay and bisexual men to ambushes by masked assailants (attacks filmed and shared); a rejected Vienna petition for queer sauna time slots; new Ministry of Education rules restricting outside sex-education providers; and Ombud guidance for gender-inclusive forms for intersex and non-binary people.

Ludwig Boltzmann Institute national report (2025) on LGBTIQ detainees in Austria, part of an EU-funded project. Covers the legal framework for LGBTIQ people in detention, gender self-determination, anti-discrimination protection, and the situation and rights of LGBTIQ people in Austrian prisons.

Austrian Justice Ministry answer to parliamentary question XXVIII. AB 774 (May-June 2025): official rules on housing transgender people in Austrian penal institutions — the authority to cite if a trans visitor is detained; German-language.

DW report (March 2025): Austrian police arrested 15 people (aged 14-26) over a wave of hate attacks in which at least 17 LGBTQ people were lured via fake dating-platform accounts to remote locations, ambushed by masked groups, filmed, and falsely accused of being paedophiles. Investigators believe the real victim count is much higher.

The Local Austria (July 2026): Austria recorded 6,751 suspected hate crimes and 7,327 prejudice motives in 2025, with 1,575 victims of prejudice-related violence; police data broken down by who faces violent hate crime, while acknowledging under-recording.

GGG (July 2026): official Austrian hate-crime statistics for the reporting year show homophobic offences rising while transphobic incidents declined — against 6,751 suspected hate crimes and 1,575 victims of prejudice-related violence in 2025 (The Local, same data).

PinkNews (Sept 2024): Austria's far-right Freedom Party (FPÖ) won the most votes in a national election for the first time since WWII (29.2%), raising concerns about what an FPÖ-led government could mean for LGBTQ+ people.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): same-sex activity legal since 1971, marriage equality since 2017, full adoption rights since 2016. Legal gender recognition is possible without mandatory medical procedures, and individuals may obtain an 'X', indeterminate, or no gender marker; intersex people can choose 'diverse', 'inter', or no designation. Equal Treatment Act covers sexual orientation, with recent amendments broadening 'gender' to include gender identity, expression and sex characteristics.

PinkNews (May 2019): Austria recognised a third gender option in official documents - intersex activist Alex Jürgen received the country's first non-binary passport ('X' marker) and birth certificate ('divers'), following the June 2018 Constitutional Court ruling that gender identity must be accurately reflected in official documents; the Interior Ministry restricted 'divers' to people with a medical panel certificate of intersexuality.

visible.summary:
Italy is broadly workable with several documented traveler-axis risks and a long-running government hostility climate. The most severe traveler-specific finding: two young transgender tourists were raped, and the convictions were confirmed on appeal in Naples in April 2026. Organised dating-app entrapment gangs have also been prosecuted (a Grindr-lure robbery gang in Padova; a 2025 assault in Bergamo).

There is documented police violence toward trans people: a Milan local-police officer was convicted in 2024 for beating a trans woman with batons in 2023. If arrested, trans women are placed in male prisons on the basis of biological sex (mitigated by a specialized section at Rome's Rebibbia prison). The Meloni government has run openly hostile rhetoric toward LGBT people for years — attacking the "LGBT lobby" and "gender ideology", and criminalising surrogacy abroad — and Italy is rated among the least progressive Western European countries on LGBT policy.

Major tourist cities (Rome, Milan, Florence) have established queer scenes and are generally safe day-to-day; bathrooms are unrestricted and there is no cross-dressing statute.
visible.tangentialFactors: Dating-app entrapment gangs (Grindr-lure robberies) are a direct caution for trans visitors using apps.
visible.localsOnly: The Rebibbia specialized prison section and the male-prison placement policy concern resident detainees; the surrogacy criminalisation is a resident-facing law.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Pickpocketing and counterfeit-goods fines affect all tourists; no trans-specific travel advisory.

sources.claim: ANSA (appeal confirmed): convictions upheld on appeal for the assault of transgender tourists in Italy — court outcome affirming accountability for violence against trans visitors.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 (covering 2025) chapter on Italy: the Education Ministry omitted LGBTI persecution from Holocaust Remembrance Day circulars for a second year; a cardinal called homosexual acts 'a mortal sin'; homophobic and transphobic violence continued including organised dating-app entrapment schemes targeting gay men; in March the Civil Court of Asti recognised for the first time physical and psychological harm from homophobic mistreatment.

Ludwig Boltzmann Institute national report (July 2025) on LGBTIQ detainees in Italy: overview of homolesbobitransphobia and discrimination, pathways to gender affirmation, same-sex relationships, and the legal/policy framework for LGBTIQ people in Italian detention.

HRW World Report 2025, Italy chapter: hostile political rhetoric about LGBT people contributing to a hostile environment, with a dedicated Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity section; broader rule-of-law and civil-society constraints noted.
tgcom24 (5 Jul 2024): Milan traffic officer sentenced to 10 months for beating a transgender woman with a baton ('trans bloccata a manganellate') — police-violence conviction against a trans person.
Progetto Gionata: transphobia in Italy as the most atroce and diffuse discrimination against transgender people — overview of the prejudice landscape facing trans people in Italy.
Outright International country overview: Italy at-a-glance — same-sex relations legal nationwide for men and women; legal matrix baseline (verify gender-recognition status in full text).
Intrepid Travel: LGBTQIA+ travel in Italy — tour-operator assessment of Italy as an LGBTQIA+ destination, practical orientation for travellers.
Frontiers in Psychiatry (2026): thematic analysis of transgender identity and psychiatric care in Italian prisons — systemic gaps and institutional challenges for incarcerated trans people.

visible.summary:
Greece is a workable destination with a clear law-versus-practice gap. The legal framework is among Europe's strongest — it ranks 7th on the ILGA-Europe Rainbow Map, has banned conversion therapy and intersex infant surgery, has a hate-crime law covering gender identity, and legalised same-sex marriage in 2024 (the first Orthodox-majority country to do so). There are no trans-specific border or bathroom restrictions, and the government is progressive with an improving trajectory.

But the social reality lags the law. A mob of about 150 people assaulted two trans people in Thessaloniki; an European Court of Human Rights case documented police detention and mistreatment of trans sex workers; surveys show Greeks are markedly more avoidant of public LGBTI visibility than the EU average (63% avoid holding hands); and the UK Foreign Office has issued an LGBTQ travel warning for Greece.

Major tourist destinations — Mykonos, Athens's Gazi district, Thessaloniki — are welcoming; outside them the climate is rougher than the law suggests.
visible.tangentialFactors: Same-sex marriage legal since 2024 — relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners; the UK Foreign Office LGBTQ travel warning is a general queer-traveler signal.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: No trans-specific travel advisory beyond the UK Foreign Office's general LGBTQ note; ordinary tourist-season crime affects all travellers.

sources.claim: ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024): marriage-equality Law 5089/2024 added SOGIESC equal-treatment guarantees in goods/services, education, healthcare and housing; in March a mob of ~150 attacked two trans people in Thessaloniki (21 arrested, 11 minors) followed by a masked attack on counter-protesters; the Orthodox Church officially opposed marriage equality; transphobic comments targeted Eurovision contestants.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 (covering 2025): the ECtHR condemned Greece for detaining an LGBTI Iranian refugee pending deportation (Article 3 violation); a criminal case opened over an online post inciting discrimination against immigrants and LGBTI people; in July the Crete Court of Appeal convicted three French tourists for a 2017 attack.

ECtHR app. 459/16, Koutra and Katzaki v. Greece (judgment 2017): police stopped and mistreated transgender sex workers and their lawyer in Athens in 2013 (street stops, removal from cars); complaints against officers were discontinued — documented police conduct toward visibly trans people.

PinkNews (Apr 2024): the UK Foreign Office updated its Greece travel advice for LGBTQ+ holidaymakers — same-sex relations legal, civil unions since 2015, marriage since Feb 2024 (first Orthodox-majority country), age of consent 15 for all, legal gender change possible; travellers advised to remain alert.

EU FRA LGBTIQ survey III, Greece country sheet (2024): 63% avoid holding hands with a same-sex partner (EU-27: 53%); 36% avoid certain locations for fear of assault (EU: 29%); only 35% are open about being LGBTIQ (EU: 51%); 28% felt discriminated at work (EU: 19%).

Outright profile (updated Mar 2026): Greece ranked 7th in Europe on the 2025 Rainbow Map; conversion practices banned for minors and IGM criminalised (2022); employment-discrimination ban on SOGI (2023); Feb 2024 Law 5089/2024 extended equal-treatment grounds (SOGIESC) across social protection, education, healthcare, housing and goods/services alongside marriage equality.

The Press Project (May 2025): TGEU Trans Rights Index & Map 2025 shows backsliding outpacing progress across Europe for the first time; Greece meets 21 of 32 indicators — gaps include age restrictions on name changes, no national action plan, no legal recognition of trans/non-binary parenthood.

Wikipedia overview: same-sex marriage legal since 2024; adoption and foster care; discrimination and hate-speech protections; self-ID gender recognition since 2017; conversion therapy; military service; social conditions including Pride events and homophobic violence.

PinkNews (Apr 2008): Justice Ministry pledged a working group on cohabiting gay couples' rights feeding upcoming unmarried-couples legislation — historical context only; superseded by civil unions (2015) and marriage equality (Feb 2024).
